article.body:
Source: Der Rebbe Redt Tzu Kinder (Second Edition) vol. 3 p. 38. Sicha of 18 Nissan, 5743.

This morning, I came one massive step closer to my ultimate goal: I, Esty from Berryville, was promoted to a three-star general! The first thing I did was make sure that everyone knew about it.

I made a new sign for my bedroom door. It says, “Esty, Three-Star General” in fancy letters that Mushkie wrote with her calligraphy pen. It’s decorated with precious stones that Baila and Yitzy, my little siblings, gathered for me from the backyard. And it’s taped onto a background of silver foil. (I thought gold foil would be more

appropriate, but my mother didn’t have any. I sure hope she gets some in time for my five- star general promotion!)

Well, it’s already 6:35 p.m., and a three-star general must get plenty of rest for the day ahead. I’m sure everyone will have lots of questions to ask me about my high-ranking position. Good night.

When I got to school, I saw another girl going to put her school bag in her locker. As the prestigious three-star general that I am, I gave her mine and said, “Locker number 302. Thank you.” and went off to class. But when I went to get my snack at recess time, I found my school bag on the floor—right in the middle of the hall.

Then, when Mrs. Feigenbaum asked for yesterday’s homework, I realized that I hadn’t finished the second page. Thinking quickly, I said, “With all due respect, Mrs.

Feigenbaum, I am a three-star general, so I am very busy.”

But Mrs. Feigenbaum just gave me an “incomplete” for the homework assignment, and with report cards coming up soon, that’s not helpful.

At lunchtime, I sat at the head of our class’s lunch table, expecting everyone to fight over who would sit near me. But everyone just sat at their usual places and chatted as always.

When I got home, I realized that I didn’t feel so good inside. The more honor I expected, the more people seemed to ignore me. I wonder if there’s a better way.

Today, Mrs. Feigenbaum took our class on a special trip to the matzah bakery.

We got to make our own matzah. It was hard work because we had to do everything fast. You only have eighteen minutes from mixing the flour and water ‘till taking the matzah out of the oven. When I help my mother make challah, she doesn’t rush like that! We leave the dough in a big bowl on the counter, covered with a towel. When we come back two hours later, the dough is a hundred times bigger.

At the bakery, we got to meet the head matzah baker, Rabbi Izzy Cohen. He asked us to tell him what’s special about matzah. I answered that matzah is special because it doesn’t rise. It’s flat and crispy.

Rabbi Izzy told us a special lesson we can learn from matzah: on

Pesach, we are careful not to eat chametz—dough that had time to rise and grow bigger. When we think too highly of ourselves, we are like chametz. On the other hand, when we are humble, we are like matzah. “No matter how great and important you become,” said Rabbi Izzy, “always try to be humble like matzah.”

That’s when it hit me. That’s what was behind my stomach ache all this time: the Yetzer Hara. He’s been trying to make me think I need lots of honor in order to feel happy and successful, but that’s not true! In fact, I think I feel a lot better when I focus on being kind and helping others instead of showing off and thinking about myself too much.

I decided to try out the humble thing because I was feeling awful. For the rest of the day, I went out of my way to think about others before myself. I tossed Yitzy a few baseballs to help him practice pitching. I gave Menucha a bath and read her a bedtime story. And when my friend Rivky called

to ask a question about homework, I gladly helped her.

My stomach ache is gone now, baruch Hashem, and I think my suspicions were correct. It’s a lot more fun to help others than to sit around all day, thinking about what everyone else can do for me.

This year’s Pesach sedarim were the best. I never ate so much matzah in my life. I’m trying to be as humble as possible, so I need all the help I can get—and what could help better than eating tons of matzah, the humblest food?

Before rachtza, Tatty told everybody that right after we say Hamotzi, we will say the special bracha for matzah: “Al achilas matzah.” We want to show that we are not eating regular bread, chas v’shalom, but pure matzah. And he asked, “Does anyone know why this is so important?”

I gladly shared the answer, I learned it in school: Pesach has two names: “Chag Hamatzos,” which means The Yom Tov of matzos, and “Zman Cheiruseinu,” which means The Time of Our Freedom.

If we act like the matzah, small and humble, then Chag Hamatzos becomes a time of freedom—free of the arrogant words of the Yetzer Hara.
